extracted.intended_audience: architects, builders, and middle-class homeowners interested in sanitary house design
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and criteria for designing, constructing, and maintaining domestic dwellings (especially middle‑class houses) with emphasis on sanitary arrangements, damp prevention, ventilation, heating, drainage, and material selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Site selection and soil treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the localities in which houses are to be situated, and the soil on which they rest; certain localities and soils are less healthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer healthy localities when possible; improve poor districts by planting and subdrainage; never enclose top soil within walls; where necessary cover subsoil with cement concrete and sometimes asphalt because damp subsoil will drive moisture up into the house. The text links soil condition to long-term accumulations of animal/vegetable matter and health risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cellar construction and use
rubrics_metrics.description: If cellars are used they must have damp-proof walls and floors, adequate light, and thorough ventilation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If cellars are constructed so water cannot pass through walls/floors, there is no need for a drain. Light and ventilation must be freely admitted; avoid sinking sickness and the concealment of defects that later produce illness or death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous damp-course over all walls
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a good damp course over the whole of the walls, internal as well as external.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damp course options: glazed earthenware perforated slabs (best if expense no object), slate courses bedded in cement above and below, asphalt on irregular ground. Avoid gas tar and sand since they deteriorate. Damp course must be placed above ground level around the building and below ground-floor joists. If there is a basement, outer walls below ground should be hollow or coated externally with an impermeable substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use impervious external materials and non-absorbent jointing
rubrics_metrics.description: Bricks and stones for external walls should be as impervious to wet as possible and jointing should be non-absorbent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid porous materials because they absorb rain and cause evaporation-driven cold. If brick/stone is non-porous but mortar is porous, water will be sucked inward at joints. Because perfectly waterproof materials are rare, pair material selection with other protections like damp courses and cavities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hollow/cavity wall construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ well-built hollow walls or provide a cavity between outer and inner portions of stone or brick walls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stone walls unless very thick should be lined with brick and a cavity left between. A half-inch cavity filled with a waterproof composition (e.g., Hygeian Rock Building Composition) can waterproof and strengthen walls and may be used as a damp course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roof performance: watertight, weathertight, and 'heat-tight'
rubrics_metrics.description: Roofs must be watertight and weathertight and should also be constructed to limit heat loss (heat-tight).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under tiles or slates provide non-conducting boarding, felt, or pugging to retain heat in winter and exclude heat in summer. Roofs should have suitable pitch to shed rain and snow. Lay boarding in narrow widths in the fall direction to avoid cockling that traps water and accelerates decay of metal gutters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eaves spouting and rainwater downpipe design and maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide ample eaves spouting and suitably spaced downpipes, with watertight joints and periodic cleaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outlets should not be contracted; protect with wire gratings to prevent blockages by leaves. Joints must be watertight to prevent sewer gas escape where downpipes connect to soil drains. Provide a siphon trap at the bottom of each downpipe unless the pipe is used as a vent; paint inside and out to prevent decay or rust; inspect and clean periodically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid continual dampness to preserve materials and health
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevent continuous humidity inside the house because it promotes chemical decay, rot, and harmful exhalations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate dry materials; avoid quickly grown timber, sour paste, stale size and wallpapers with injurious pigments. Plaster and mortar must be free from organic matter and salts, since these produce nitrates/deliquescent salts that attract moisture and deteriorate finishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful selection of materials for mortar and plaster (no sea-sand or organic contaminants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Materials for mortar and plaster should be as free from salts and organic matter as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sea sand or sand containing salt; avoid road drift in plaster; organic matter in plaster leads to formation of salts and moisture attraction, causing blistering, peeling, and unhealthy exhalations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architect's active supervision and testing of materials/apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: Architects must watch work from sod-cutting to finishing touches and test the value of materials and apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architects should ensure instructions are intelligently executed by trustworthy workmen and check that sanitary details are carried out; many unsanitary conditions result when defects are covered and only discovered after illness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heating method selection and air-change necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose heating methods that minimize waste, dirt, and health hazards while ensuring constant air change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open fires are wasteful, dirty and can create unhealthy draughts and imperfect combustion; ventilating grates help but do not fully solve waste/smoke issues. Closed stoves are more economical but risk charging the atmosphere with combustion products; slow-combustion stoves reduce this risk. Any heating system (steam, hot water, heated air) demands special and adequate ventilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central heating (steam/hot water) advantages and ventilation needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Steam/hot-water central heating can be efficient and allow boilers to be remote, but requires adequate ventilation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steam allows heating multiple dwellings and cooking services from a distant furnace; when using steam or hot water ensure special ventilation measures are in place to prevent accumulation of combustion products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gas stoves and pipes: placement, leakage, and ventilation concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Gas stoves can be convenient but are often expensive and difficult to prevent combustion products entering the dwelling; gas pipes should be accessible for inspection and repair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gas leakages can taint soil and indoor air; pipes embedded in plaster are hard to inspect/repair—prefer laying pipes where they can be exposed for inspection. Reference: in France pipes are left exposed except where unavoidable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artificial lighting contamination and preference for electricity
rubrics_metrics.description: All combustion-based lighting (candles, oil, gas) contaminates the air; electric lighting is preferable as technology improves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gas especially can contaminate atmosphere and furniture and leakages from mains can be hard to detect. The hope is for future electric improvements to reduce atmospheric contamination in homes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kitchen arrangement and fume extraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Cooking ranges should be constructed to carry off fumes and kitchens must be well ventilated and sited so fumes do not enter other parts of the house.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condensed volatile cooking products can deposit on walls/furniture and later putrefy. Design ranges and flues to remove cooking fumes; avoid routes that allow smells to permeate the home.

rubrics_metrics.name: Washhouse placement and steam removal
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the washhouse away from the living parts of the house or ventilate it well and provide a proper boiler/flue to carry off steam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Washing day steam and stifling air can permeate the building, reducing comfort; architect can lessen the problem by siting and ventilating laundry spaces properly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refuse disposal: eliminate exposed ash-pits
rubrics_metrics.description: Do away with conventional ash-pits that collect organic matter and putrefy; use covered removable receptacles emptied frequently or promptly burn refuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend galvanized iron covered receptacle on wheels emptied every 2–3 days; where gardens exist provide distant composting space. Burning refuse promptly (in ranges or open fires managed well) is preferable to allowing rotting which causes health hazards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privies, cesspools and earth closets: siting, ventilation, and watertightness
rubrics_metrics.description: Privies and cesspools must be sited distant from dwellings, frequently emptied, well ventilated, and watertight; earth closets can be used indoors if carefully attended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cesspools are worse in crowded neighborhoods; watertightness is critical to prevent groundwater contamination and disease. Avoid placing rainwater tanks under dwellings because sewage may find its way through drains. Earth closets require reliable disposal systems in towns; the water closet is acceptable if properly constructed and maintained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water-closet (w.c.) design: avoid pan closets; use large-pan with water seal and S-trap
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject the old pan closet; prefer a large pan retaining a water layer swept by flush water and connected to an S-trap with ventilating outlet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pan closets are known to be defective; funnel-shaped pans are objectionable because they trap dirt. From the S-trap take the soil pipe immediately through the wall and connect to a strong watertight 4 in iron pipe continued above windows, with a ventilating trap at its foot to cut air connection with drains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wastes from baths, sinks and urinals: ventilation and disconnection
rubrics_metrics.description: Wastes should be ventilated and disconnected from drains or allowed to discharge above a gulley trap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper ventilation/disconnection prevents foul air return; excrement and other wastes must be quickly removed from premises to keep homes 'sweet'.

rubrics_metrics.name: House-drain materials and jointing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use well-burnt, well-glazed, twist-free glazed stoneware pipes and carefully make joints of cement or well-tempered clay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lay pipes on concrete if ground is not firm; wipe away all projecting portions from the inside of pipes to ensure a clear passage-way. Badly joined or irregular pipes cause matter accumulation, fermentation and sewer-gas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drain layout: straight lines, man-holes/lamp-holes, and accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Lay drains in straight lines from point to point and insert man-holes or lamp-holes at each angle or intersection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Straight runs and man-holes make examination, flushing, and ventilation easy, and quick removal of stoppages possible. The Local Government Board insists on this for public buildings, and it is recommended for house-drains too.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide disconnecting trap before entry to main sewer
rubrics_metrics.description: Each house drain should have a disconnecting trap just before it enters the main sewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents air connection between house-drains and the main sewer and stops sewer-gas developed elsewhere being allowed into the house. Also use ventilating traps to cut air connection entirely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure proper trenching, falls, and bedding to prevent sinking and blockages
rubrics_metrics.description: Trenches should be excavated to proper falls, and pipes bedded on a layer of concrete to prevent sinking where ground is soft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper falls keep drains self-cleansing; incorrect laying causes foul drains from settling, irregularity, and accumulation. Avoid curved angles in drains which are less good than straight lines with inspection openings.
